The lack of access to clean cooking costs Africa USD 791 billion every year in health, economic, and environmental losses. This is equivalent to around one fifth of the continent’s GDP.
 
I was pleased to contribute to the Africa Regional Forum on Sustainable Development 12, where we discussed how accelerating clean cooking can unlock broader development outcomes.
 
Clean cooking is one of the highest-return investments available today. The question is no longer whether we can afford it, but whether we can afford not to.
 
What is changing now is how the sector is being transformed through three structural shifts:
 
First, data and digital tools to scale solutions.
Geospatial tools, AI, and digital platforms are helping map demand, monitor usage, and align supply with real needs. In Rwanda, where access stood at just 8 percent in 2022, a data-driven pathway now projects over 3.4 million households adopting clean cooking solutions by 2029.
 
Second, building markets at scale.
Sub-Saharan Africa needs around USD 4 billion annually by 2030, yet investment remains far below this. Clean cooking must be treated as an economy to build, with investable pipelines that unlock public and private finance.
 
Third, integrating clean cooking into energy planning.
In Kenya and Uganda, e-cooking tariffs are making electric cooking more affordable by aligning policy with real household demand. This is the direction of the UNDP–AFREC Beyond Stoves initiative, advancing policy reform, gender-responsive institutions, and market development.
 
With Mission 300 gaining momentum, the Clean Cooking Summit in Kenya and the SDG7 review at the High-Level Political Forum in 2026 will be a window of opportunity for the clean cooking agenda.
 
Through #UN-Energy, which brings together more than 30 UN entities, we have a platform to align efforts, strengthen coherence, and accelerate delivery across the system.

UNDP stands ready to support countries in moving from ambition to implementation, so that clean cooking becomes a financed, gender-responsive, and coordinated pillar of Africa’s development pathway.
